# SCADA Harmonization & Contextualization Service

A data harmonization pipeline that transforms heterogeneous industrial SCADA telemetry into standardized, ISA-95-aligned canonical messages for enterprise analytics and Unified Namespace (UNS) streaming architectures.

## Problem

Industrial telemetry systems suffer from:

- **Inconsistent naming** — camelCase, snake_case, hyphenated keys across sources
- **Varied JSON structures** — flat vs nested vs topic-based identity
- **Disparate units** — bpd vs m³/day, psi vs kPa, °F vs °C
- **Inconsistent status codes** — "P", "RUN", "Producing" mean the same thing
- **Unreliable timestamps** — ISO strings, epoch seconds, milliseconds, or missing
- **No contextual hierarchy** — lack of ISA-95 alignment

This fragmentation blocks cross-site KPI standardization, enterprise analytics, reliable streaming, M&A integration, and trustworthy AI applications.

## Solution

This service provides a centralized harmonization layer that:

1. Ingests events from multiple heterogeneous SCADA sources
2. Extracts ISA-95 contextual hierarchy (Enterprise → Site → Area → Cell → Equipment)
3. Normalizes units (m³/day → bpd, kPa → psi, °C → °F)
4. Standardizes status codes to a canonical enum
5. Validates telemetry constraints with strict Pydantic models
6. Emits canonical, enterprise-aligned events
7. Generates UNS-compatible topic structures
8. Provides full mapping lineage and explainability
9. Routes invalid events to dead-letter with structured errors

## Architecture

```
Input JSON → Source Adapter → Raw Extracted → Transform Layer → Canonical Model → UNS Envelope
```

See [docs/ARCHITECTURE.md](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) for detailed design and [docs/PRD.md](docs/PRD.md) for full requirements.

## License

MIT

1	# AGENTS.md
2	
3	This file provides guidance to WARP (warp.dev) when working with code in this repository.
4	
5	## Project Overview
6	
7	SCADA Harmonization Service — a Python pipeline that transforms heterogeneous industrial SCADA telemetry (from 3 different legacy source formats) into standardized, ISA-95-aligned canonical messages for enterprise analytics and Unified Namespace (UNS) streaming. The project is currently in a **pre-implementation state** (documentation only, no source code yet).
8	
9	## Key Documentation
10	
11	- `docs/PRD.md` — Full product requirements with fixture examples and acceptance criteria
12	- `docs/ARCHITECTURE.md` — Pipeline architecture, Pydantic model hierarchy, component design
13	- `docs/IMPLEMENTATION_PLAN.md` — Milestone breakdown (M0–M8) with planned project structure and tasks
14	
15	## Planned Project Structure
16	
17	When implementation begins, the package lives under `src/scada_harmonizer/` with this layout:
18	- `cli.py` — Typer-based CLI entry point
19	- `pipeline.py` — Pipeline orchestrator
20	- `models/` — Pydantic models: `sources.py`, `canonical.py`, `envelope.py`, `errors.py`, `lineage.py`
21	- `adapters/` — Source-specific adapters (`source_a.py` CygNet, `source_b.py` Wonderware, `source_c.py` Ignition) + `registry.py`
22	- `transforms/` — `units.py`, `status.py`, `timestamps.py`
23	- `uns/` — `namespace.py` (InMemoryUNS), `topics.py`, `wildcards.py`
24	- `writers/` — `jsonl.py`
25	- `tests/` at project root
26	- `fixtures/` at project root with `source_a/`, `source_b/`, `source_c/`, `equivalence/` subdirs
27	
28	## Build and Development Commands
29	
30	```
31	# Dependencies (planned)
32	# pyproject.toml with: pydantic>=2.0, typer, pytest, pytest-cov
33	
34	# Install in dev mode
35	pip install -e ".[dev]"
36	
37	# Run tests
38	pytest
39	
40	# Run a single test
41	pytest tests/test_adapters.py::test_source_a_valid
42	
43	# Run with coverage
44	pytest --cov=scada_harmonizer
45	
46	# CLI usage (planned)
47	scada-harmonize run --input fixtures/ --output output/
48	scada-harmonize query "exxon/+/+/+/esp/+/telemetry"
49	```
50	
51	## Architecture: Data Flow
52	
53	```
54	Input JSON → Source Detection (discriminated union) → Adapter → RawExtractedEvent → Transform Layer → CanonicalTelemetry → UNS Envelope → InMemoryUNS
55	                                                                                          ↓ (validation failure)
56	                                                                                    DeadLetterEntry → dead_letter.jsonl
57	```
58	
59	Every data boundary is a Pydantic model. No raw dicts cross layer boundaries.
60	
61	## Three Source Formats
62	
63	| Source | Style | Key Traits |
64	|--------|-------|------------|
65	| A (CygNet) | Flat JSON, compound tag name | Imperial units, short status codes ("P"/"S"/"X"), ISO timestamps |
66	| B (Wonderware) | Flat JSON, discrete fields | Metric units (m³/day, kPa, °C), verbose statuses, epoch seconds |
67	| C (Ignition) | Nested JSON with MQTT topic | Topic-embedded ISA-95 identity, mixed units, epoch milliseconds |
68	
69	Source auto-detection uses Pydantic discriminated union on payload shape: `topic` key → Source C, `wellId` → Source B, `tag` → Source A.
70	
71	## Critical Design Constraints
72	
73	- **Pydantic-first**: All models use Pydantic v2. Use `Field(alias=...)` in source models, discriminated unions for routing, `field_validator`/`model_validator` in canonical models, constrained types (`ge`, `le`) for ranges, `model_serializer` for UNS envelope output.
74	- **ISA-95 hierarchy** is required on all canonical events: Enterprise → Site → Area → Cell → Equipment Class → Equipment ID.
75	- **Canonical units are imperial**: m³/day → bpd (×6.28981), kPa → psi (×0.145038), °C → °F (×9/5+32).
76	- **Status normalization**: All sources map to enum `Producing`/`ShutIn`/`Offline`/`Unknown`. Unmapped codes → `Unknown` (never raise).
77	- **Deterministic transforms**: Same input must always produce same output.
78	- **Cross-source equivalence**: The same physical event from any source must produce identical canonical output — this is the core proof of harmonization.
79	- **Report-by-exception**: UNS only emits when values change from retained state.
80	- **Birth certificates**: First event per device emits a full-state snapshot to `.../birth` topic.
81	- **Dead-letter routing**: Invalid events go to `dead_letter.jsonl` with structured Pydantic `ValidationError` details, never silently dropped.
82	
83	## Equipment Classes
84	
85	Two supported: `Well` (flow_rate_bpd, tubing_pressure_psi, temperature_f) and `ESP` (intake_pressure_psi, motor_temperature_f, motor_current_amps, vibration_ips). Each has class-specific measurement fields and range constraints defined in the canonical model.
86	
87	## Testing Strategy
88	
89	- **Unit tests**: Conversion functions, status mapping, timestamp parsing, range validation, data quality flags
90	- **Integration tests**: Valid/broken fixtures through full pipeline
91	- **Cross-source equivalence tests**: Same physical event from all 3 sources → identical canonical output
92	- **UNS tests**: Retained state, report-by-exception, birth certificates, wildcard matching (`+` single level, `#` remaining levels)
93	- **Edge cases**: Missing optional fields, null required fields, out-of-range values, empty payloads, duplicate events
94	
95	## Output Files
96	
97	- `output/canonical.jsonl` — Successfully harmonized events (only changed values per report-by-exception)
98	- `output/dead_letter.jsonl` — Rejected events with structured errors and original payload

1	# Industrial Semantic Harmonization Engine (ISHE)
2	## ER&I AI Innovation Challenge Submission
3	
4	**Version:** v3 | **Date:** 2026-02-20
5	**Submission deadline:** February 24, 2026
6	
7	---
8	
9	## Q1. Innovation Title
10	
11	**Industrial Semantic Harmonization Engine (ISHE): The Universal Translator for Industrial Data**
12	
13	> "We cannot sell high-value AI consulting if our clients' data is trapped in cryptic SCADA tags. We must build the 'Universal Translator' to unlock the market."
14	
15	---
16	
17	## Q2. Problem Statement
18	
19	### The Heart of the Business Problem
20	
21	Every industrial AI initiative — predictive maintenance, autonomous operations, digital twins, GenAI copilots — is blocked by the same upstream obstacle: **millions of cryptic, inconsistent, undocumented SCADA tags that machines cannot understand.**
22	
23	A pump discharge pressure reading appears as all of the following across a single enterprise:
24	
25	```
26	P101_DISCH_PRESS        (Plant A — CygNet)
27	Pump-101.DischargePSI   (Plant B — Wonderware)
28	P_101_PD                (Plant C — FactoryTalk)
29	pump101.pressure.out    (Plant D — Ignition/MQTT)
30	POMPE_101_PRESSION_REF  (Plant E — French acquisition)
31	```
32	
33	These are the same physical measurement. A human engineer recognizes this instantly. A machine, without context, cannot. This "metadata problem" is the single largest barrier to scaling AI, analytics, and Unified Namespace (UNS) architectures across the industrial sector.
34	
35	### Cross-Sector Evidence
36	
37	Active engagements shaping the OT data harmonization problem at **ExxonMobil** (~$615B market cap, upstream O&G), **Arkema** (~$5B market cap, specialty chemicals), and **ERCOT** (independent system operator managing ~90% of Texas's electrical load) reveal a consistent common thread: the inability to harmonize operational technology (OT) data and use it for integrated analytics across IT, OT, and engineering technology (ET) domains. Three organizations, three sectors, one problem.
38	
39	### Sector-Specific Trigger Events
40	
41	| Sector | Trigger Event | The Problem |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| Upstream & Midstream O&G | M&A consolidation wave ($150B+ in 4 mergers within 12 months) | 50,000+ tags per acquisition require 24–36 months of manual migration; $3–4B in annual Pioneer synergies delayed per year of integration backlog |
44	| Downstream & Chemicals | Open Process Automation (OPA/O-PAS) migration | 200,000+ tags per facility; misclassified SIS alarm = regulatory incident or plant shutdown |
45	| Power & Utilities | DER integration (solar/wind/battery growing 20–30% annually) | Every inverter OEM uses different SCADA tag structures; mapping backlog grows faster than staffing |
46	| Discrete Manufacturing | Industry 4.0 / cloud migration | "Machine State" encoded differently at every site; enterprise-wide OEE and predictive maintenance blocked |
47	
48	*Adjacent market context:* The global SCADA market is projected at $12.9B in 2025 growing to ~$20B by 2030 [15]; the oil and gas SCADA segment specifically reaches $5.5B by 2030 [18]; and the broader IT/OT integration market grows from $51.9B (2023) to $133.7B by 2030 [17]. ISHE targets the semantic mapping pain point inside these programs — a fraction of total spend that yields the $4.5–10B TAM estimate in Q3.
49	
50	### Impacted Clients, Personas, and Stakeholders
51	
52	| Persona | Role | Primary Pain Point |
53	|---|---|---|
54	| OT Integration Engineer | Manages SCADA-to-enterprise data flows post-M&A | 50,000 tags, 24–36 months of manual mapping on a spreadsheet |
55	| Control Room Manager | Remote operations from Central Remote Operations Center | Cannot trust tags across acquired assets; alarm fatigue from misclassified alarms |
56	| Data / Analytics Engineer | Builds ML models and KPIs on historian data | De-contextualized tags arriving in the data lake are unusable for AI; manual cleaning per project |
57	| CDO / GBS Lead | Governs enterprise data standards globally | No single arbiter of industrial data semantics at scale; every acquisition resets the problem |
58	| Process Safety Engineer | ISA-18.2 and IEC 61511 compliance | Tag migration can misclassify safety-critical alarms; one error = regulatory incident |
59	| M&A Integration Lead | Captures structural cost savings post-acquisition | $3–4B in annual Pioneer synergies blocked per year of unresolved tag migration backlog |
60	
61	---
62	
63	## Q3. Expected Business Impact
64	
65	### Client Impact
66	
67	**Revenue Growth**
68	- *Industry benchmark:* ExxonMobil's Vantage platform has demonstrated a 29,000 bpd production uplift through field and remote operations optimization enabled by standardized SCADA data [1] — establishing the measurable value of harmonized OT data that ISHE is designed to unlock across future acquisitions
69	- *Industry benchmark:* Autonomous ESP optimization in the Permian Basin has demonstrated 2–4% oil uplift and extended equipment run life when sensor data is clean and semantically consistent [2] — the foundational condition ISHE is built to provide
70	
71	**Cost Reduction**
72	- Expected to reduce engineering effort per acquired well from 4–8 hours (manual) to under 1 hour (automated) — projecting a 6–8× reduction in integration labor cost across a typical large-scale acquisition (internal estimate based on industry-standard OT integration labor rates)
73	- Goodnight Midstream: UDT-based edge modeling with Moxa AIE gateways reduced equipment onboarding from a half-day effort to 20 minutes [3]
74	
75	**Risk Mitigation**
76	- Will eliminate alarm misclassification risk during tag migration — ISA-18.2 alarm rationalization lineage preserved end-to-end through the canonical model
77	- Will maintain IEC 61511 SIS integrity — dead-letter routing flags every tag that cannot be confidently resolved, preventing silent misclassification of safety-critical signals
78	- Per-field lineage will enable full regulatory audit of every transformation applied to every canonical field
79	
80	**Experience Improvement**
81	- OT integration engineers will move off spreadsheets — mapping effort redirected to high-value architecture and validation work
82	- Control room operators will be able to trust standardized tags across acquired assets; alarm fatigue projected to be eliminated
83	- Data/analytics engineers will receive ISA-95-aligned canonical data directly into Snowflake — ML pipelines will no longer be broken by acquisition events
84	- GenAI copilots and operator assistants will become viable because the underlying data is semantically rich
85	
86	### Scale Potential for the Firm
87	
88	| Metric | Value |
89	|---|---|
90	| Total Addressable Market | $4.5–10B annually [15] (upstream O&G, downstream, chemicals, power/utilities, manufacturing; internally derived, directionally supported by published market data — see Q2) |
91	| Year 1 revenue | $9–15M (3–5 engagements, building the library) |
92	| Year 4 revenue | $50–80M+ (25–40 engagements, 70% gross margins, licensing upside) |
93	| Active cross-sector demand signal | ExxonMobil, Arkema, ERCOT — 3 organizations, 3 sectors, 1 problem |
94	
95	The firm that establishes a defensible semantic library in the next 24 months will be positioned as the foundational layer for industrial AI for the next decade. A Year 4 revenue target of $50–80M represents less than 2% of the stated TAM [15] — a modest share for a specialized, differentiated capability at market entry.
96	
97	### Likely Client Count (Conservative Scale View)
98	
99	Beyond TAM, I estimated a **serviceable client universe of ~20–35 ER&I organizations** where SCADA semantic harmonization is a near-term need (internal estimate based on what I have seen in the last two months).
100	
101	- **Near-term pilot pool (next 12 months):** 8–15 likely clients
102	- **Realistic Year 1 conversion:** 2–4 paying clients
103	- **3–4 year active-client potential:** 15–25 clients
104	
105	These ranges assume conservative pilot-to-paid conversion.
106	
107	---
108	
109	## Q4. Proposed AI Solution
110	
111	### Trigger
112	
113	An M&A integration, OPA migration, or UNS deployment exposes tag chaos — thousands of assets publishing semantically inconsistent telemetry to a central platform that cannot interpret it.
114	
115	### Three-Tier Hybrid AI Architecture
116	
117	```
118	                ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
119	Incoming Tags ──→│      Tier 1: Deterministic       │──→ 60–70% resolved
120	                │  Regex + Suffix Rules + Lookup   │    (high confidence)
121	                └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
122	                               ↓ (unresolved)
123	                ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
124	                │      Tier 2: NLP / Fuzzy         │──→ 20–25% resolved
125	                │  Statistical matching + Embeddings│    (medium confidence)
126	                └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
127	                               ↓ (still unresolved)
128	                ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
129	                │    Tier 3: Contextual GenAI      │──→ 5–10% resolved
130	                │  P&ID parsing + Document RAG     │    (requires human review)
131	                └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
132	                               ↓
133	                ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
134	                │    Human-in-the-Loop Review      │──→ <5% manual resolution
135	                │  Engineer confirms/corrects      │
136	                └──────────────┬──────────────────┘
137	                               ↓
138	                ┌─────────────────────────────────┐
139	                │        Feedback Loop             │
140	                │  Confirmed mappings feed back    │
141	                │  into Tier 1 & 2 training data   │
142	                └─────────────────────────────────┘
143	```
144	### Steps → Output → User Value
145	
146	| Step | Activity | Detail |
147	|---|---|---|
148	| 1 | Source Detection | Auto-detect source system (CygNet, Wonderware, Ignition) from payload shape; extract ISA-95 hierarchy from compound tag names or MQTT topic paths |
149	| 2 | Three-Tier Resolution | Tier 1 deterministic → Tier 2 NLP/fuzzy → Tier 3 contextual GenAI, each with confidence scoring and dead-letter routing for failures |
150	| 3 | Normalization | Units (m³/day→bpd, kPa→psi, °C→°F), status codes (P/RUN/Producing → canonical enum), timestamps → UTC |
151	| 4 | Canonical Validation | Pydantic-enforced type and range constraints; cross-field checks (e.g., zero flow while "Producing" → `Suspect` flag); per-field quality scoring |
152	| 5 | UNS Publication | ISA-95 topic hierarchy (enterprise/site/area/cell/equipment_class/equipment_id/category); retained state; report-by-exception; birth certificates on first contact |
153	| 6 | Feedback Loop | Confirmed mappings promoted to Tier 1 rules or Tier 2 training set; library grows with each engagement |
154	
155	**Outputs:**
156	- Canonical JSONL — Snowflake-ingestible via `COPY INTO`
157	- UNS topic hierarchy — queryable with MQTT-style wildcards (`exxon/permian/+/+/esp/#`)
158	- Dead-letter log — every invalid payload preserved with structured field-level errors and original payload snapshot
159	- Per-field lineage — each canonical field carries full provenance back to source key, original value, and conversion applied
160	- Data quality scores — `Good` / `Suspect` / `Bad` with descriptive flags per event
161	
162	**User value by persona:**
163	
164	| Persona | Before | After |
165	|---|---|---|
166	| OT Integration Engineer | 24–36 months of manual spreadsheet mapping | 3–6 months automated; spreadsheet replaced by lineage log |
167	| Control Room Manager | Alarm fatigue; distrust of acquired asset tags | Standardized tags, ISA-18.2 lineage, zero misclassification |
168	| Data / Analytics Engineer | De-contextualized tags in Snowflake; manual cleaning | Canonical JSONL with ISA-95 context lands ready for ML |
169	| CDO / GBS Lead | No arbiter of industrial semantics at scale | Compounding library is the semantic standard |
170	| Process Safety Engineer | Migration risk of misclassifying SIS alarms | Dead-letter routing preserves every safety-critical tag for review |
171	| M&A Integration Lead | Savings blocked by tag backlog | 6× faster integration; savings captured within the same fiscal year |
172	
173	### Compounding Advantage
174	
175	By the 5th engagement in a given sector, 85%+ of tags resolve automatically without human intervention. The library is the intellectual property. The engine is the delivery mechanism.
176	
177	| Engagement | Tags Mapped | Reuse Rate on Next Engagement |
178	|---|---|---|
179	| Client 1 (Upstream O&G) | 50,000 | — |
180	| Client 2 (Midstream) | 30,000 | ~70% |
181	| Client 3 (Chemicals) | 45,000 | ~75% |
182	| Client 4 (Power & Utilities) | 25,000 | ~80% |
183	| Client 5 (Manufacturing) | 60,000 | ~85% |
184

187	## Q5. POC Level of Effort
188	
189	**Rating: MEDIUM (4–8 weeks)**
190	
191	**POC scope:** ExxonMobil/Pioneer CygNet integration — one source type (CygNet), one equipment class (Well), synthetic fixtures representing Pioneer Permian Basin tag naming conventions. No live SCADA connection required.
192	
193	### Week-by-Week Milestones
194	
195	| Week | Milestone | Key Deliverable |
196	|---|---|---|
197	| 1 | M0 — Foundation | Project skeleton (pyproject.toml, package structure, CLI); CygNet fixture files — valid wells, broken variants, cross-source equivalence set |
198	| 2 | M1 — Canonical Model | `WellTelemetry` Pydantic model with ISA-95 identity, range constraints, and cross-field validators; `DataQuality` and `DeadLetterEntry` models |
199	| 3 | M2 — Source Adapter | CygNet adapter: compound tag name → ISA-95 hierarchy extraction; `RawExtractedEvent` intermediate model; source auto-detection |
200	| 3–4 | M3 — Error Handling | Dead-letter handler (catch `ValidationError`, preserve original payload, extract field-level errors); JSONL writers |
201	| 4–5 | M4 — Transform Layer | Unit conversion (exact constants); status normalization; timestamp→UTC; per-field lineage records |
202	| 5–6 | M5 — Pipeline | End-to-end CLI (`scada-harmonize run`); batch processing with summary report (processed / succeeded / dead-lettered counts) |
203	| 6–8 | M6 partial — UNS | Topic builder (ISA-95 → sanitized lowercase hyphenated topic); in-memory retained state; birth certificate emission; report-by-exception; wildcard query CLI |
204	
205	### Measurable Success Metrics
206	
207	1. Tier 1 deterministic resolution resolves ≥ 60% of tags with zero false positives
208	2. Identical canonical output for the same physical event arriving from different source formats (cross-source equivalence test passes)
209	3. 100% of invalid payloads produce structured dead-letter entries with original payload preserved and field-level error detail
210	4. Deterministic, sanitized, ISA-95-aligned UNS topics for all valid events
211	5. `scada-harmonize query "exxon/permian/+"` returns live namespace state after batch processing

236	| Cloud platforms (AWS SiteWise, Azure Digital Twins) | Cloud-native modeling | Require data to already be clean and contextualized; they don't solve the upstream mapping problem | Engine solves the mapping problem first, then feeds any cloud platform with canonical, ISA-95-aligned output |

238	### Market Gap
239	
240	> "Existing tools help you model clean data and have limited native  support to clean fragmented OT data at scale"
241	
242	The Industrial Semantic Harmonization Engine fills the gap that every tool on this list — and every industrial AI initiative — requires as a prerequisite. It is not a competitor to any of these platforms. It is the layer that makes all of them viable. The broader IT/OT integration market — projected to reach $133.7B by 2030 [17] — consistently identifies data integration and semantic interoperability as the foundational prerequisite layer, validating the gap ISHE fills.

246	## Q8. Minimum Data Requirements
247	
248	### Source Data Formats Supported
249	
250	**Source A — CygNet-style flat JSON** (compound tag name, imperial units, short status code, ISO timestamp):
251	```json
252	{
253	  "tag": "PERMIAN_NORTH_PAD12_WELL_E77",
254	  "flow": 1250.5,
255	  "pressure": 3200.0,
256	  "temp": 185.0,
257	  "status": "P",
258	  "ts": "2024-03-15T14:30:00Z"
259	}
260	```
261	
262	**Source B — Wonderware-style flat JSON** (discrete field names, metric units, verbose status, epoch seconds):
263	```json
264	{
265	  "wellId": "E-77",
266	  "site": "Permian",
267	  "area": "North",
268	  "pad": "Pad-12",
269	  "flowRate_m3d": 198.8,

274	}

277	**Source C — Ignition/MQTT nested JSON** (hierarchical structure, topic-embedded identity, epoch milliseconds):
278	```json

280	  "topic": "Exxon/Permian/North/Pad-12/ESP/E-77/telemetry",
281	  "payload": {

292	### Unit Conversion Requirements
293	
294	| Source Unit | Canonical Unit | Conversion Factor |
295	|---|---|---|
296	| m³/day | bpd | × 6.28981 |
297	| kPa | psi | × 0.145038 |
298	| °C | °F | (× 9/5) + 32 |
299	
300	### POC Minimum Data Requirements
301	
302	- ≥ 100 tag events per source type
303	- ≥ 3 equipment instances per source
304	- ≥ 1 broken record per source (dead-letter routing verification)
305	- ≥ 1 duplicate event per device (report-by-exception suppression verification)
306	- ≥ 1 cross-source equivalence set (same physical Well E-77 event in Source A and B formats — must produce identical canonical output)
307	- File-based ingestion only; no live SCADA connection required for POC
308	
309	### Production Integration Requirements
310	
311	| Component | Requirement |
312	|---|---|
313	| MQTT broker | Live UNS publication (HiveMQ, EMQX, or Ignition MQTT Engine) |
314	| Historian API | Bulk tag export from CygNet, Wonderware, OSIsoft PI for initial migration |
315	| P&ID documents | PDF ingestion for Tier 3 RAG-based contextual resolution |
316	| Maintenance / work order system | SAP PM or equivalent for Tier 3 RAG |
317	| Target data lake | Snowflake (canonical JSONL via `COPY INTO`) or AWS IoT SiteWise for canonical output streaming |
318

321	## Q9. Additional Criteria
322	
323	### Build vs. Buy: Four-Zone Analysis
324	
325	| Zone | Approach | Platform / Tool |
326	|---|---|---|
327	| Data Transport / MQTT | Leverage existing | Ignition MQTT Engine, HiveMQ, EMQX |
328	| Edge Contextualization | Leverage existing (as transport framework) | HighByte Intelligence Hub |
329	| **Semantic Resolution Engine (Tiers 1–3)** | **Custom Build** | No existing product performs AI-assisted tag mapping with a compounding cross-client semantic library |
330	| Enterprise Storage / Output | Leverage existing | Snowflake (COPY INTO from canonical JSONL), AWS IoT SiteWise |
331	
332	### Why the Core Engine Is a Custom Build
333	
334	No existing product performs AI-assisted industrial tag mapping with a **compounding cross-client semantic library**:
335	
336	- **HighByte Intelligence Hub:** Excellent edge transport and manual model-building framework — but engineers must define the information model manually per site. That bottleneck is exactly what ISHE eliminates.
337	- **OSIsoft PI AF:** Historian-specific; does not resolve tags from heterogeneous source systems. Creates vendor lock-in.
338	- **LLMs in isolation (GPT-4, Claude):** Can propose tag mappings from a prompt but do not maintain a persistent, compounding cross-client semantic library. Every prompt starts from zero.
339	- **Cloud platforms (AWS IoT SiteWise, Azure Digital Twins):** Require data to arrive pre-labeled and pre-contextualized. They are the destination, not the solution to the upstream mapping problem.
340	
341	### POC Technology Stack
342	
343	| Component | Technology |
344	|---|---|
345	| Data modeling and validation | Python + Pydantic v2 |
346	| CLI / pipeline orchestration | Typer |
347	| Tier 1 — Deterministic resolution | Python regex + lookup tables |
348	| Tier 2 — NLP / fuzzy matching | Sentence-transformers or spaCy |
349	| Tier 3 — Contextual GenAI | LangChain + Claude or GPT-4 (API) |
350	| UNS simulation | In-memory Python dict (MQTT semantics simulated) |
351	| Output | JSONL (Snowflake-ingestible via `COPY INTO`) |
352	
353	### Firm AI Platform Compatibility
354	
355	Tier 3 GenAI inference routes through the firm's existing OpenAI or AWS Bedrock platform — **no new AI infrastructure required**. Tiers 1 and 2 are fully self-contained and deployable on any Python environment without shared AI infrastructure. The deterministic Tier 1 has zero external dependencies beyond the semantic library itself.

# Industrial Semantic Harmonization Engine (ISHE)
## ER&I AI Innovation Challenge Submission

**Version:** v3 | **Date:** 2026-02-20
**Submission deadline:** February 24, 2026

---

## Q1. Innovation Title

**Industrial Semantic Harmonization Engine (ISHE): The Universal Translator for Industrial Data**

> "We cannot sell high-value AI consulting if our clients' data is trapped in cryptic SCADA tags. We must build the 'Universal Translator' to unlock the market."

---

## Q2. Problem Statement

### The Heart of the Business Problem

Every industrial AI initiative — predictive maintenance, autonomous operations, digital twins, GenAI copilots — is blocked by the same upstream obstacle: **millions of cryptic, inconsistent, undocumented SCADA tags that machines cannot understand.**

P_101_PD                (Plant C — FactoryTalk)
pump101.pressure.out    (Plant D — Ignition/MQTT)
POMPE_101_PRESSION_REF  (Plant E — French acquisition)
```

Industrial plants run heterogeneous SCADA systems where the *same physical measurement* shows up under dozens of cryptic, inconsistent tag names, units, status codes, and timestamp formats:

A Python pipeline that ingests telemetry from 3 legacy source formats and emits standardized, **ISA-95-aligned canonical events**:

- **Dead-letter routing** — invalid events preserved with structured field-level errors, never silently dropped.
- **Per-field lineage** — full provenance/explainability for every transformation.

Equipment classes: `Well` and `ESP`. Stack: Python + Pydantic v2 + Typer CLI + pytest. ### Note 1: Hand-built Sparkplug B UNS

### Simulating cryptic PLC memory or tag names

## Python libraries and modules

### Core Python modules for the project

The core Python stack should center on Pandas for data shaping, Paho MQTT for MQTT transport, PySparkplug for Sparkplug B publishing, and DuckDB for developer-friendly analytical SQL over Parquet and replayed datasets.[cite:67][cite:90][cite:100][cite:151] If ERPNext and Neo4j are part of the lab, Python should also be used for enterprise integration services and graph-loading or graph-query services because that keeps the custom implementation surface consistent across the architecture.[cite:90][cite:92][cite:97][cite:227][cite:233][cite:238][cite:242]

One practical sequence is:

1. Load and replay benchmark datasets through Python.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151]
2. Add synthetic operational and actuator context.[cite:151][cite:156]
3. Convert the values into PLC-like tags or OpenPLC-facing structures.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:167]
4. Publish them into MQTT / Sparkplug B.[cite:78][cite:90][cite:100][cite:104]
5. Consume them in SCADA, historian, and dashboard layers.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:35][cite:39][cite:40]
6. Feed selected business-relevant events into ERPNext.[cite:227][cite:233]
7. Feed selected semantic and event relationships into Neo4j.[cite:234][cite:238][cite:242]

That combination makes the home lab stronger as both a learning environment and an architecture prototype, because it demonstrates not only how to collect industrial data but how to harmonize, contextualize, and operationalize it across SCADA, historian, analytics, enterprise, graph, and cloud-style domains with largely open-source or free tools.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:35][cite:39][cite:68][cite:80][cite:185][cite:227][cite:233][cite:238]

- The **harmonization layer maps PLC tags → Sparkplug B metrics + ISA-95 asset paths**, preserving traceability and carrying units, asset class, site/line context, and IDs that tie into enterprise/graph entities.

### The target stack (full enterprise landscape)
- **MQTT / Sparkplug B** as the UNS backbone
- **SCADA** (Ignition), **historian** (InfluxDB/Timescale), **dashboards** (Grafana), **analytics/ML** (Kafka, DuckDB, Python)
- **ERPNext** — the SAP-like enterprise application layer
- **Neo4j** — the connected-context knowledge graph spanning OT ↔ enterprise
- **floci** — local AWS-style IT/cloud emulation

### Three implementation routes under consideration (the other 3 design notes)
1. **Hand-built Sparkplug B UNS** — assemble every component manually, open-source (max learning, every boundary explicit).
2. **UMH-anchored** — United Manufacturing Hub Community as the backbone (fastest to end-to-end demo).
3. **Python-centric** — same architecture, but Python is the primary implementation language across replay, synthetic generation, Sparkplug publishing, enrichment, ERPNext + Neo4j integration.

### Canonical execution sequence
replay benchmark data → add synthetic operational context → disguise as PLC tags → publish to MQTT/Sparkplug B → consume in SCADA/historian/dashboards → feed events to ERPNext → feed relationships to Neo4j → reuse for ML/edge/cloud via floci.

---

So the `docs/` ISA-95/Pydantic pipeline is really *one slice* (the harmonization engine) of a much larger home-lab vision — which is probably the source of the confusion you mentioned.

I'm ready for the next note. Which would you like — the three architecture options (`hand_built`, `umh_anchored`, `python_centric`) or `synthetic_data_generation`?

content.content:
1	# Hand-Built Sparkplug B UNS Notes
2	
3	These notes describe a hand-built home-lab architecture for a Sparkplug B-centered Unified Namespace (UNS) using only open-source tools or free/community editions, with no dependency on United Manufacturing Hub as the backbone.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:21][cite:33][cite:68][cite:78][cite:185] The intent is to understand each architectural layer directly by assembling the components yourself, while still keeping the design realistic enough that paid or enterprise alternatives can later replace individual parts without invalidating the overall model.[cite:39][cite:45][cite:68][cite:80][cite:89]
4	
5	## Purpose
6	
7	The hand-built path is best when the goal is to learn the moving parts of a modern industrial data architecture rather than start from a platform bundle.[cite:68][cite:71][cite:78] Instead of inheriting MQTT, Kafka, storage, dashboards, and modeling from UMH, this architecture defines each role explicitly so you can understand what each component contributes to the final plant-to-cloud story.[cite:68][cite:71][cite:89]
8	
9	This architecture is still intended to be realistic.[cite:89] It keeps only Level 0 synthetic, represents Level 1/2 through PLC-world structures, uses Sparkplug B to harmonize that data into an MQTT-based UNS, stores and analyzes it in OT and IT layers, and uses floci to emulate the AWS-shaped enterprise cloud side locally.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:78][cite:89][cite:182][cite:185]
10	
11	## Architectural summary
12	
13	A concise summary of the hand-built architecture is:
14	
15	1. **Level 0**: benchmark datasets plus Python-generated signals represent sensors, actuators, and operating context.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151]
16	2. **Level 1/2**: OpenPLC or a PLC-like memory/tag structure represents controller-facing integration.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:167]
17	3. **Level 3 transport and harmonization**: MQTT broker plus Sparkplug B structure create the UNS backbone.[cite:68][cite:78][cite:89]
18	4. **Level 3 OT systems**: Ignition Maker Edition or trial, historian/TSDB, and Grafana consume or store operational data.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:35][cite:40]
19	5. **Level 3/4 streaming and analytical infrastructure**: Kafka or equivalent plus Parquet/object storage and DuckDB build the IT analytics path.[cite:39][cite:45][cite:67][cite:72]
20	6. **Level 4 cloud/IT emulation**: floci emulates AWS-style object storage, streaming, orchestration, and analytics services locally.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]
21	7. **Cross-cutting**: Python services handle replay, synthetic generation, mapping, enrichment, analytics, and inference publishing.[cite:90][cite:92][cite:100][cite:104]
22	
23	Unlike the UMH-anchored pattern, there is no platform that pre-bundles these roles.[cite:80][cite:112] Every service is selected and wired intentionally, which is both the main challenge and the main educational benefit.[cite:68][cite:71][cite:89]
24	
25	## Why choose the hand-built path
26	
27	The hand-built route is useful when the project needs transparency, portability, and deep understanding.[cite:68][cite:71] It makes the interfaces between controller data, MQTT/Sparkplug harmonization, storage, event streaming, analytics, and IT/cloud patterns visible rather than abstracted away.[cite:78][cite:89]
28	
29	This matters because a Unified Namespace is easy to talk about conceptually but only becomes concrete when you explicitly decide:
30	
31	- Where the semantic mapping happens.[cite:162][cite:166]
32	- What owns historian storage versus event streaming.[cite:35][cite:39][cite:45]
33	- How OT applications and IT applications each consume the same harmonized signals.[cite:84][cite:89]
34	- How cloud-style data products are fed from the industrial event backbone.[cite:73][cite:182][cite:185]
35	
36	With a hand-built lab, each of those decisions becomes visible and testable.[cite:68][cite:89]
37	
38	## Level 0: Synthetic and benchmark process reality
39	
40	Only Level 0 should be synthetic in this design.[cite:145][cite:150] Benchmark datasets and Python-generated signals create realistic sensor, actuator, and equipment-state behavior, but everything above that point should behave like a real OT/IT stack.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151][cite:167]
41	
42	The recommended dataset strategy is:
43	
44	- Use the **Industrial IoT Dataset (Synthetic)** for machine-oriented equipment behavior such as motors, compressors, conveyors, or predictive-maintenance style assets.[cite:145]
45	- Use the **Tennessee Eastman Process** dataset for process-oriented multivariable behavior such as tanks, reactors, loops, and fault scenarios.[cite:150][cite:155]
46	- Add Python-generated contextual signals such as valve state, run mode, counts, downtime, and OEE-style indicators that most benchmark datasets do not provide directly.[cite:151][cite:156]
47	
48	This gives the lab both realistic process dynamics and operational context.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151] It also supports a strong story: only the physical world is simulated, while the PLC, messaging, storage, analytics, and cloud-like layers are real software systems configured as a production-like stack.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:68][cite:185]
49	
50	## Level 1/2: PLC-world representation
51	
52	### OpenPLC and PLC-style tags
53	
54	OpenPLC is a strong open-source stand-in for a PLC because it supports industrial controller concepts and can expose data over protocols such as Modbus TCP.[cite:21][cite:33] Even when values are generated in Python, they should be shaped to look like PLC memory addresses or cryptic controller tags before being published into the broader data stack.[cite:163][cite:167][cite:169]
55	
56	Examples of this include:
57	
58	- Address-based identifiers such as `N7:20`, `MW100`, or `DB10.DBD4`.[cite:167]
59	- Cryptic tag names such as `FIC101_PV`, `P201_RUNFB`, or `MTR04_AMP`.[cite:163][cite:169]
60	
61	This level is important because many real plants do not expose a semantic model at the control layer.[cite:163][cite:167] They expose memory maps, sparse naming conventions, and controller-specific structures that later need harmonization.[cite:162][cite:168]
62	
63	### Why this matters to the UNS story
64	
65	If the lab skipped the PLC-world layer and sent friendly semantic names directly from Python into MQTT, it would lose one of the core educational lessons of a UNS: the transition from cryptic, source-system data to clean, enterprise-usable data.[cite:162][cite:166][cite:168] Keeping the PLC-world layer visible makes Sparkplug B and the harmonization process meaningful rather than cosmetic.[cite:78][cite:89][cite:162]
66	
67	## Sparkplug B and MQTT as the backbone
68	
69	### Broker choices
70	
71	The recommended open-source MQTT broker choices are:
72	
73	- **Mosquitto**, for a minimal, lightweight lab broker.[cite:68]
74	- **EMQX OSS**, for a more feature-rich industrial IoT broker with an easier path to enterprise editions later.[cite:68][cite:70]
75	
76	Either broker can serve as the central MQTT transport layer for the UNS.[cite:68] EMQX OSS is often the better choice if the lab wants more broker-like features, while Mosquitto is easier when minimal footprint and simplicity matter more.[cite:68]
77	
78	### Why Sparkplug B instead of plain MQTT JSON
79	
80	Sparkplug B provides a consistent industrial topic and payload model with node and device births, metric aliases, datatypes, and lifecycle awareness.[cite:78][cite:166] That structure is what elevates MQTT from a generic pub/sub fabric to a real industrial messaging and harmonization layer.[cite:78][cite:89][cite:168]
81	
82	In a hand-built architecture, Sparkplug B is especially useful because it prevents every publisher and consumer from inventing incompatible ad hoc conventions.[cite:78][cite:89] It gives a standard contract for how controller-derived values become reusable UNS metrics across SCADA, historian, analytics, and cloud-style consumers.[cite:84][cite:89][cite:166]
83	
84	### Python Sparkplug services
85	
86	Python should be the default implementation language for custom publishers and replay services in this architecture.[cite:90][cite:92][cite:100] The core Python transport stack is:
87	
88	- **Paho MQTT** for MQTT connectivity.[cite:90][cite:99]
89	- **PySparkplug** for Sparkplug B publishing and metric modeling.[cite:100][cite:104][cite:105]
90	
91	This lets the hand-built architecture remain highly flexible: Python can replay benchmark data, publish births and updates, consume UNS topics, enrich data, and later publish inference results back into the same semantic structure.[cite:92][cite:97][cite:100][cite:104]
92	
93	## SCADA and OT consumers
94	
95	### Ignition’s role
96	
97	Ignition Maker Edition or trial is a good fit as the main SCADA/HMI tool in the hand-built stack.[cite:3][cite:6] It is the same platform used commercially, which means any UDT structures, screens, or consumption patterns developed in the lab can carry forward into a paid deployment.[cite:3][cite:6]
98	
99	In this architecture, Ignition should be treated as an OT consumer of the UNS rather than the owner of the UNS itself.[cite:84][cite:89] That means Sparkplug and MQTT define the industrial data backbone, while Ignition validates that an OT application can consume harmonized data for visualization, alarming, and operator-facing applications.[cite:81][cite:84]
100	
101	### Historian choices
102	
103	A hand-built architecture needs an explicit historian choice because no platform bundle is making that decision for you.[cite:35][cite:39][cite:40] Good free/open-source options include:
104	
105	- **InfluxDB OSS** for a simple, strong time-series option with a clear cloud/enterprise path later.[cite:35][cite:40]
106	- **TimescaleDB Community** if PostgreSQL compatibility and relational joins matter.[cite:39][cite:48]
107	- **QuestDB OSS** if high-ingest, SQL-oriented time-series access is attractive.[cite:37][cite:45]
108	
109	The choice depends on the rest of the lab. Timescale is especially appealing if you already use Postgres or want stronger SQL semantics; InfluxDB is convenient when the historian is primarily operational time-series storage.[cite:35][cite:39][cite:48]
110	
111	### Grafana as visualization
112	
113	Grafana OSS is a natural dashboard and trending layer for the hand-built architecture.[cite:40][cite:45] It can sit beside Ignition rather than replace it: Ignition provides SCADA-style views, while Grafana gives broader engineering and analytical trends across historian and IT-side data sources.[cite:40][cite:45]
114	
115	## Streaming, batch, and analytics path
116	
117	### Kafka or equivalent
118	
119	A hand-built UNS architecture benefits from having an explicit streaming backbone on the IT side, even if MQTT remains the plant-side transport.[cite:39][cite:45][cite:73] Apache Kafka OSS is the most natural choice because it is widely used for streaming pipelines and has direct analogs in managed enterprise platforms.[cite:39][cite:45]
120	
121	Kafka’s role here is not to replace MQTT or Sparkplug in OT.[cite:73][cite:89] Its role is to support downstream analytics, stream processing, lake ingestion, event replay, and enterprise integration once data leaves the immediate OT context.[cite:39][cite:45][cite:73]
122	
123	### Batch and lakehouse pattern
124	
125	A practical pattern is:
126	
127	- MQTT/Sparkplug in OT for plant-side real-time semantics.[cite:78][cite:89]
128	- Historian/TSDB for operational time-series retention.[cite:35][cite:39][cite:40]
129	- Kafka for event streaming to IT.[cite:39][cite:45]
130	- Parquet files in object storage for batch analytics and ML feature creation.[cite:67][cite:72]
131	- DuckDB for developer-friendly analytical SQL over Parquet.[cite:67][cite:72]
132	
133	This layered approach keeps operational and analytical needs separated while still allowing them to consume the same harmonized signals.[cite:39][cite:45][cite:72][cite:89]
134	
135	### DuckDB’s role
136	
137	DuckDB is a strong choice for IT-side analytics in a lab because it works extremely well with Parquet and local workflows.[cite:67][cite:72] It is especially useful for:
138	
139	- Feature exploration and ad hoc analytical SQL.
140	- Joining historian exports with business context.
141	- Producing training datasets for ML.
142	- Prototyping data products before moving them to managed warehouse or lakehouse services.[cite:67][cite:72]
143	
144	DuckDB is not the operational historian and not the MQTT backbone.[cite:67][cite:72] Its role is the analytical query engine that sits beside the streaming and storage layers.
145	
146	## Neo4j knowledge graph integration
147	
148	### Why add Neo4j in the hand-built stack
149	
150	Neo4j is a strong addition when the lab should include a **knowledge graph** that captures relationships across assets, tags, events, maintenance history, production context, and enterprise objects rather than relying only on time-series and relational stores.[cite:238][cite:242] Knowledge-graph approaches are increasingly used for digital-twin-style data integration because they represent connected industrial context well across heterogeneous systems.[cite:234]
151	
152	In the hand-built architecture, Neo4j should be treated as a connected-context layer, not as a replacement for the MQTT broker, historian, or ERP.[cite:89] Its role is to preserve and query the relationships between physical assets, semantic metrics, anomalies, work orders, material flow, and maintenance actions in a way that complements the rest of the stack.[cite:234][cite:239]
153	
154	### What Neo4j should model
155	
156	A practical graph model for this lab should include nodes such as:
157	
158	- **Site, area, line, cell, and asset** for physical hierarchy.
159	- **PLC tag / source tag** for cryptic controller-facing identifiers.[cite:163][cite:167]
160	- **Metric / signal** for Sparkplug or derived semantic variables.[cite:166][cite:168]
161	- **Event** for faults, downtime, alarms, batches, and maintenance-triggering conditions.
162	- **ERP objects** such as work orders, assets, materials, and stock movements once ERPNext is integrated.[cite:227][cite:233]
163	
164	The graph should emphasize relationships such as `PART_OF`, `HAS_METRIC`, `GENERATED_EVENT`, `TRIGGERED_MAINTENANCE`, `FULFILLS_WORK_ORDER`, and `CONSUMED_MATERIAL`.[cite:234][cite:239] Those relationships make it easier to answer cross-domain questions that are awkward in a historian alone.
165	
166	### Where Neo4j sits in the hand-built stack
167	
168	Neo4j should sit on the **IT / context / reasoning side** of the hand-built architecture, downstream of Sparkplug-harmonized data and alongside ERP/integration services.[cite:234][cite:239] A good mental model is:
169	
170	1. Level 0 replay/generation creates plant behavior.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151]
171	2. PLC-world structures preserve source realism.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:163][cite:167]
172	3. MQTT + Sparkplug create the harmonized UNS backbone.[cite:68][cite:78][cite:166]
173	4. Historian and SCADA layers consume operational data.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:35][cite:39]
174	5. Integration services write selected context into ERPNext and Neo4j.[cite:227][cite:233][cite:238]
175	6. Neo4j ties OT structure, event history, and ERP context into a graph suitable for advanced querying and graph-assisted applications.[cite:234][cite:239]
176	
177	This keeps concerns separated: the broker carries events, the historian stores time series, ERPNext owns business records, and Neo4j owns connected context.[cite:89][cite:227][cite:234]
178	
179	### How Neo4j integrates with Sparkplug, OT data, and ERPNext
180	
181	Neo4j should consume from the **harmonized** side of the architecture rather than from raw unstructured source values whenever possible.[cite:78][cite:89][cite:166] In practical terms, Python or other integration services should subscribe to Sparkplug topics or Kafka-fed derivatives and use those to populate graph entities and relationships.[cite:39][cite:45][cite:90][cite:238]
182	
183	That allows the graph to preserve useful traceability such as:
184	
185	- PLC/source tag to semantic metric mappings.[cite:163][cite:167][cite:168]
186	- Asset to event and event to downtime/fault relationships.[cite:234]
187	- Work order to line, machine, batch, and output relationships once ERPNext is connected.[cite:227][cite:233]
188	- Maintenance action to anomaly, runtime threshold, or failure event relationships.[cite:233][cite:234]
189	
190	This is one of the most practical reasons to add Neo4j: it creates a connected layer spanning OT and enterprise records without forcing everything into one schema or one database style.[cite:234][cite:239]
191	
192	### Python and Neo4j in the hand-built stack
193	
194	Even though this note is architecture-centric rather than Python-centric, Python remains the most practical custom integration language for Neo4j because Neo4j provides an official Python driver and Python is already present elsewhere in the lab for replay, data preparation, and analytics.[cite:90][cite:92][cite:238][cite:242] That makes it straightforward to build graph-loading and graph-update services without introducing a separate integration language purely for the graph layer.
195	
196	### GraphRAG and future use cases
197	
198	Neo4j also creates an upgrade path toward GraphRAG or graph-assisted operational copilots.[cite:239][cite:245] Neo4j’s GraphRAG tooling for Python is meant to combine graph relationships with retrieval workflows, which could later support troubleshooting assistants, lineage queries, maintenance reasoning, and impact analysis across the industrial stack.[cite:245]
199	
200	### Neo4j resource links
201	
202	- Neo4j Python driver GitHub: <https://github.com/neo4j/neo4j-python-driver> [cite:238]
203	- Neo4j Python driver on PyPI: <https://pypi.org/project/neo4j-driver/> [cite:242]
204	- Neo4j GraphRAG Python package: <https://github.com/neo4j/neo4j-graphrag-python> [cite:245]
205	
206	## ERP / SAP-like integration with ERPNext
207	
208	### Why ERPNext fits the hand-built architecture
209	
210	ERPNext is a strong open-source stand-in for SAP-like enterprise integration because it is positioned as open-source ERP software for manufacturing and can represent manufacturing, inventory, and broader operational business context in one platform.[cite:227][cite:233] For the scope you identified—production, maintenance, logistics, and manufacturing—it is a practical enterprise-side destination for harmonized OT data in this lab.[cite:227][cite:233]
211	
212	In the hand-built Sparkplug B UNS design, ERPNext should sit on the **enterprise / business application side** of the stack, downstream of the harmonized OT data backbone.[cite:89][cite:227] It should not receive every raw telemetry value; instead, it should receive curated operational events and business-relevant updates derived from the UNS.[cite:89][cite:227]
213	
214	### What OT data should flow into ERPNext
215	
216	Good ERPNext integration targets in the lab include:
217	
218	- **Production / manufacturing**: work-order confirmations, completed counts, scrap counts, runtime and downtime summaries, batch completion, and line-state-based production milestones.[cite:227]
219	- **Maintenance**: maintenance-triggering events, anomaly summaries, runtime thresholds, equipment condition indicators, and failure/downtime classifications.[cite:233]
220	- **Logistics / inventory**: material consumption, finished-goods completion, inventory adjustments, WIP movement, and transfer-style events inferred from line activity.[cite:227][cite:233]
221	
222	This is a realistic ERP integration pattern because enterprise systems like SAP or ERPNext usually consume curated transactions and events rather than high-frequency raw tag streams.[cite:89][cite:227]
223	
224	### How ERPNext integrates into the hand-built stack
225	
226	A practical hand-built ERPNext flow is:
227	
228	1. Replay and synthetic services generate realistic plant behavior.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151]
229	2. PLC-world structures preserve source-system realism.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:163][cite:167]
230	3. Sparkplug B and MQTT create the harmonized UNS layer.[cite:68][cite:78][cite:166]
231	4. SCADA and historian systems consume that data operationally.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:35][cite:39]
232	5. Python or other integration services consume selected harmonized events and write business-relevant updates into ERPNext.[cite:90][cite:227][cite:233]
233	
234	In this role, ERPNext becomes the SAP-like enterprise system for work execution feedback, maintenance records, inventory/logistics context, and manufacturing state beyond the OT layer.[cite:227][cite:233]
235	
236	### Why ERPNext is useful in this lab
237	
238	Adding ERPNext makes the hand-built architecture more complete because it demonstrates how a UNS feeds enterprise systems rather than stopping at dashboards and historians.[cite:89][cite:227] It gives a realistic destination for production confirmations, maintenance workflows, and material/logistics events and therefore strengthens the plant-to-enterprise story of the lab.[cite:227][cite:233]
239	
240	### ERPNext resource links
241	
242	- ERPNext manufacturing overview: <https://frappe.io/erpnext/open-source-manufacturing-erp-software> [cite:227]
243	- ERPNext GitHub repository: <https://github.com/frappe/erpnext> [cite:233]
244	
245	## floci as the cloud/IT emulation layer
246	
247	### Why include floci in a hand-built design
248	
249	floci is a free, open-source local AWS emulator with support for a broad set of AWS-shaped APIs and services, including S3, Lambda, Kinesis, MSK, Glue, Athena, EventBridge, Step Functions, RDS, and more.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185] In the hand-built architecture, floci becomes the cloud-side landing zone that makes the lab look like it feeds enterprise cloud patterns without needing an actual AWS account.[cite:182][cite:185]
250	
251	This matters because the hand-built path is not only about OT basics.[cite:89] It is also about showing a full plant-to-enterprise pattern where the UNS can drive cloud-style data lake, analytics, orchestration, and ML workflows.[cite:73][cite:182][cite:185]
252	
253	### Specific roles floci can play
254	
255	#### 1) S3-style data lake
256	
257	floci’s S3 emulation can receive Parquet or CSV snapshots exported from Kafka consumers, historian exports, or Python pipelines.[cite:182][cite:185] This gives the lab a cloud-shaped data lake for long-term analytical storage and lakehouse-style workflows.[cite:185]
258	
259	#### 2) Kinesis/MSK-style streaming destination
260	
261	floci can emulate Kinesis and MSK, making it possible to test how UNS-derived streams might be forwarded into AWS-style enterprise eventing patterns.[cite:185] This is especially useful if the long-term target architecture includes managed streaming or cloud-native data products.
262	
263	#### 3) Lambda and Step Functions
264	
265	floci’s Lambda and Step Functions support can emulate event-driven processing, scheduled transformations, and orchestration workflows.[cite:182][cite:185] This is useful for:
266	
267	- Triggering feature calculations on new data drops.
268	- Running enrichment or alerting functions.
269	- Orchestrating model training, scoring, or backfill routines.
270	
271	#### 4) Glue and Athena
272	
273	Glue and Athena emulation make it possible to catalog and query object-store data in an AWS-shaped way.[cite:185] This complements DuckDB: DuckDB is ideal for local development and fast iteration, while floci emulates the cloud service interfaces an enterprise data team may later adopt.[cite:67][cite:72][cite:185]
274	
275	#### 5) RDS and OpenSearch
276	
277	floci’s RDS and OpenSearch endpoints can be used for downstream application patterns such as metadata storage, curated marts, or searchable event logs.[cite:185] These are optional but useful when the lab should show that a UNS can feed not just historians and dashboards, but many application and platform services.[cite:89][cite:185]
278	
279	### Where floci sits in the stack
280	
281	In the hand-built architecture, floci should sit clearly on the IT/cloud side, not in the OT transport path.[cite:182][cite:185] A clean separation looks like this:
282	
283	- **OT side**: OpenPLC, Python replay/generation, MQTT broker, Sparkplug B, Ignition, historian.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:68][cite:78]
284	- **Bridge layer**: Kafka consumers, historian exports, Python ETL or stream processors.[cite:39][cite:45][cite:72]
285	- **IT/cloud side**: floci S3, Athena, Lambda, EventBridge, Kinesis, RDS, and related services.[cite:182][cite:185]
286	
287	This makes the cloud side a consumer and processor of harmonized industrial data rather than a replacement for the OT messaging model.[cite:89][cite:185]
288	
289	## Python’s role across the stack
290	
291	Python is the best language to standardize on in this hand-built architecture because it can span nearly every custom part of the system.[cite:90][cite:92][cite:100] Useful Python roles include:
292	
293	- Replaying benchmark datasets in time order.[cite:145][cite:150][cite:151]
294	- Generating additional analog and discrete signals.[cite:151][cite:156]
295	- Injecting realistic messiness such as spikes, missing points, and state transitions.[cite:136][cite:141][cite:156]
296	- Mapping benchmark variables to PLC tags and PLC tags to Sparkplug metrics.[cite:163][cite:167][cite:100]
297	- Publishing and consuming MQTT/Sparkplug streams.[cite:90][cite:99][cite:100][cite:104]
298	- Consuming Kafka and writing Parquet or cloud-emulated outputs.[cite:39][cite:67][cite:72][cite:185]
299	- Training models and deploying inference services that publish predictions back into the UNS.[cite:71][cite:97][cite:101]
300	
301	This makes the hand-built design highly coherent: infrastructure components are open-source services, and Python is the implementation layer that ties them together.[cite:68][cite:90][cite:100]
302	
303	## Recommended end-to-end flow
304	
305	A practical end-to-end sequence for the hand-built lab is:
306	
307	1. Load the Industrial IoT and TEP datasets in Python.[cite:145][cite:150]
308	2. Generate missing operational context such as valve state, machine mode, counts, and OEE-related signals.[cite:151][cite:156]
309	3. Inject modest realism issues such as missing points, spikes, and manual-mode behavior.[cite:136][cite:141][cite:156]
310	4. Map those values into PLC-style addresses or cryptic controller tags.[cite:163][cite:167]
311	5. Publish them as Sparkplug B node and device metrics via MQTT.[cite:78][cite:100][cite:104]
312	6. Consume the harmonized signals in Ignition and write history into a TSDB.[cite:3][cite:6][cite:35][cite:39]
313	7. Forward selected streams into Kafka and write analytical copies to Parquet/object storage.[cite:39][cite:45][cite:67][cite:72]
314	8. Use DuckDB and/or floci services such as Athena, Lambda, or S3 for IT/cloud-style analytics and orchestration.[cite:67][cite:72][cite:182][cite:185]
315	9. Train ML models and deploy Python scoring services that publish enriched or predictive metrics back into the Sparkplug B UNS.[cite:71][cite:97][cite:100][cite:101]
316	
317	This loop demonstrates both OT-to-IT data flow and IT-to-edge feedback, which is critical if the lab is meant to show actual operationalization of analytics and ML rather than just passive dashboards.[cite:71][cite:73][cite:101]
318	
319	## Upgrade path and realism
320	
321	One reason this hand-built design is valuable is that it is upgrade-friendly.[cite:68][cite:89] Each open-source or free component has an obvious replacement path later if the project moves toward production:
322	
323	- Mosquitto or EMQX OSS can be replaced by EMQX Enterprise, HiveMQ, or cloud MQTT brokers while preserving MQTT/Sparkplug contracts.[cite:68][cite:89]
324	- Ignition Maker/trial can be replaced by licensed Ignition without changing the application model.[cite:3][cite:6]
325	- InfluxDB OSS or Timescale Community can be replaced by cloud or enterprise offerings.[cite:35][cite:39]
326	- Kafka OSS can move to Confluent or managed Kafka services.[cite:39][cite:45]
327	- floci endpoints can move to actual AWS services later with much smaller changes than a redesign would require.[cite:182][cite:184][cite:185]
328	
329	That means the hand-built lab is not just educational; it is also a prototype architecture with a credible path toward real deployment patterns.[cite:68][cite:89][cite:185]
330	
331	## Practical links
332	
333	### Data and core tools
334	
335	- Industrial IoT Dataset (Synthetic): <https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/canozensoy/industrial-iot-dataset-synthetic> [cite:145]
336	- Tennessee Eastman Process data: <https://dataverse.harvard.edu/dataset.xhtml?persistentId=doi%3A10.7910%2FDVN%2F6C3JR1> [cite:150]
337	- OpenPLC references: [cite:21][cite:33]
338	- Paho MQTT: <https://pypi.org/project/paho-mqtt/> [cite:90]
339	- PySparkplug: <https://github.com/matteosox/pysparkplug> [cite:100]
340	
341	### OT and UNS infrastructure
342	
343	- Ignition Maker Edition docs: <https://www.docs.inductiveautomation.com/docs/8.1/other-editions/ignition-maker-edition> [cite:6]
344	- EMQX open-source info: [cite:68]
345	- Sparkplug specification: [cite:78]
346	- Grafana OSS references: [cite:40][cite:45]
347	- Timescale and historian references: [cite:39][cite:48]
348	- InfluxDB historian references: [cite:35][cite:40]
349	- DuckDB: <https://duckdb.org/> [cite:67]
350	
351	### Cloud/IT emulation
352	
353	- floci site: <https://floci.io/floci/> [cite:185]
354	- floci GitHub: <https://github.com/floci-io/floci> [cite:180]
355	
356	## Working conclusion
357	
358	The hand-built Sparkplug B UNS scenario is the right option when the goal is to assemble and understand the full industrial data architecture yourself: synthetic Level 0 reality, PLC-world source structures, Sparkplug B harmonization, explicit MQTT and historian choices, explicit OT and IT consumption paths, and a local cloud emulation layer through floci.[cite:21][cite:33][cite:68][cite:78][cite:89][cite:185]
359	
360	It is more work than a UMH-anchored design, but it gives deeper understanding of where each concern belongs and makes every integration surface visible.[cite:68][cite:71][cite:89] That makes it especially valuable for learning, for architecture experimentation, and for building a stack that can later swap individual components for paid or enterprise equivalents without losing the design principles established in the lab.[cite:39][cite:45][cite:68][cite:182][cite:185]
